stories.title: Wynona’s diary years
stories.status: editorial prototype; claims and rights await Beth’s review
stories.opening: In 1879, an eleven-year-old in the Drumore circle began collecting words from relatives and friends. Eleven years later, Jessie Wynona Lamborn began a diary. Its pages move between school, worship, travel, weather, friendship and loss. This story follows five moments in that surviving account, with the archive trail beside each one.
stories.ending: The diary continues beyond these five moments. Here, Wynona’s own words and the family archive offer a route through a particular year, not a complete account of her life. Beth’s review of the diary, identities, captions and permissions is the next editorial step.

scenes.title: An autograph book
narrative: At eleven, Wynona began an autograph book. The pages gathered advice and affection from relatives and friends, making a small record of the people around her before she kept a diary.

One photographed spread carries messages signed by her uncle Aquilla Lamborn and other family members. The archive account describes more than forty pages, but the complete book and its ownership still need Beth’s review.
scenes.evidenceNote: The 1879 year and relationship identifications come from Beth’s archive post. The photographed spread itself includes a March 17, 1879 inscription; it does not date every page in the book.

scenes.title: Beginning the diary
narrative: On her twenty-second birthday, Wynona opened a diary with a reason to write: she hoped to look back on pleasant things while remembering that life also held loss. She recorded a rainy autumn day and an evening drive to her aunt and uncle’s new house.

The archive account places her teaching at the Conowingo School and staying with relatives during the school week. Those biographical details are useful context, but they need checking against the diary and other records before publication.
scenes.quote: This being my twenty-second birthday, I thought it would be a good time to start a diary.
scenes.evidenceNote: The quoted opening is Beth’s transcription in P045. The pictured cover and title page are original diary photographs; this prototype has not independently compared every transcription line with the manuscript.

scenes.title: A week at Institute
narrative: In November, Wynona traveled to Lancaster for a week of teachers’ institute lectures, music and friends. Her entries name the people she roomed with and the speakers she heard; they also record a persistent toothache.

The postcard shows Millersville State Normal School, where Beth says Wynona had trained. It gives the scene educational context, but the diary account places this institute week and lodging in Lancaster; the postcard should not be read as a photograph of that week.
scenes.evidenceNote: The month comes from candidate event E030. Beth’s transcription in P054 supplies daily entries from November 9–16, 1890. The school postcard is contextual archive material, not a dated image of Wynona’s trip.

scenes.title: Winter entries
narrative: The diary keeps moving through ordinary winter life: worship, school, visitors, music, illness, bad roads and snow. On Christmas Day Wynona counted presents and described an evening with Early Earnhart. On December 26 she noted heavy snow and sleet; the following day people were out sleighing.
These entries feel close to daily life, but the twelve linked posts cover a wider period from December into February. The scene gives that span honestly rather than collapsing it into a single day.
scenes.quote: Very heavy snow fell last night, and continued all day with sleet, making very good sleighing.
scenes.evidenceNote: The scene range is December 1890–February 1891. Beth’s posts include transcribed daily entries, with P063 and P064 providing the details highlighted here. A sleigh photograph in P063 is undated contextual imagery and is intentionally not presented as a record of Wynona’s ride.

scenes.title: News of Isaac
narrative: By spring, Wynona’s diary had recorded sickness and deaths in the community. On April 16 she wrote that Isaac Bolton Shoemaker had died that evening after much suffering. The archive account connects him to Wynona’s extended circle and follows his family history in a separate post.

The photographed grave marker offers a different kind of evidence from the diary transcription. Together they support a question for Beth: confirm the date, family relationships and cemetery record from the original sources before this story is published.
scenes.quote: Altho’ looked for by all it seemed sudden.
scenes.evidenceNote: P093 contains Beth’s transcription of Wynona’s April 16 entry; P092 provides the family account and grave image. The grave photograph’s capture date and cemetery location are not established in this selected metadata.

entries.label: 12 Oct 1890, continued
entries.text: … to keep. To-day has been dull and rainy, the leaves falling, covering the ground, as a reminder that winter is approaching. All hail! To Autumn, in which there is something so expressive to me. Uncle, Aunt [Thomas and Lib Hambleton] and I, home all day, till evening I came down to Uncle Will’s [William L. Shoemaker]. Had a dark and rainy drive, but not a lonesome one. This evening the first I spent in their new house. They moved in on Oct. 11. As far as a nice home goes, they have every advantage.

entries.label: Oct. 13.
entries.text: Nothing particular happened to-day. Had my regular school duties to attend to. Learned this wk. of {Groff’s} Mill being burned on Oct. 8, about 8 P.M. Much damage done. To-day is still dull, and very cold and raw air.

entries.label: Oct. 14.
entries.text: Just came home from school. Cleared about noon to-day, with wind in West, having a clear, bracing feeling in the air. The new book-case arrived at the school-house. Cost $6.00. To-day finished my second month of school. Last eve Neal & Sallie Hambleton made a call.

entries.label: Oct. 15.
entries.text: After I came home from school went up to Uncle Jacob’s, and spent about 1 hr. talking with Aunt Sallie and Mamie. Had a pleasant day at school. First load of coal hauled for winter. Weather is very clear and cool, drying up mud very fast.

transcriptions.note: Page 1 of 3. Original spelling kept (“greatful,” “layed”). A repeated “and” is struck through in the original. If the letter dates from 1873, as P035 says, it speaks of both parents as living, which fits the 1874 death date for Phebe (P057).

entries.label: Page 1
entries.text:
My Dearly beloved daughter thy fathers and Mothers lives are just wearing out, and ere many months pass away, the Sun of their lives will have set; and thee will behold them no more on Earth in their material forms; and dear Child, knowing that I am poor in what is called worldly possessions & the probabilities are that I cannot bequeath to thee any property of that nature, I feel greatful that there is a wealth which I can and will cheerfully give to thee, that thee may use it daily during thy natural life and ~and~ be abundantly rewarded; and when thy sojourn on earth is ended, thee will receive thy great reward in the Summerland.

I enjoin it upon thee, Dear Child, to follow well the advice herein layed down, and thee cannot go much astray from the path of duty to thyself and to others.
